Paul Graham essay filler. The art of writing great software is the art of writing a program that other people can easily understand and modify. Good code is not merely correct; it is legible, and its structure reveals intent at a glance. Most of the time I spend programming is not spent typing, but thinking about how to shape the problem so that the code writing itself becomes almost mechanical.

When I was younger I believed that the most important skill in programming was inventiveness. I now believe the most important skill is restraint. The code you do not write is cheaper to maintain than the code you do. Every abstraction has a carrying cost, and many abstractions that look like they pay for themselves at the time turn out to be expensive over years.

I have spent a lot of time thinking about the relationship between simplicity and correctness. Simple programs are easier to reason about, and programs that are easier to reason about are more likely to be correct. But simplicity is not the same as brevity — terse code can be extraordinarily complex, and verbose code can be extraordinarily simple. The simplicity that matters is simplicity of the mental model, not of the text.

One heuristic I've developed: if a function cannot be renamed to something accurate and short, it is probably doing too many things. Splitting such functions almost always improves the code, not because of any formal principle, but because the act of naming each part forces you to think about what each part actually is.

Filler content about medieval cartography. Early maps were not primarily navigational tools but philosophical objects, ordering the known world around theological centers like Jerusalem. The T-O map, so named for its characteristic shape, divided the world into three continents separated by waters forming a T inside an O. These maps do not lie: they simply encode a different theory of what a map is for.

The rise of portolan charts in the 13th and 14th centuries marked a shift toward empirical geography. Portolans were working documents for sailors, annotated with coastlines, wind rose grids, and compass bearings. Their accuracy along familiar coasts was astonishing, even if their interior territories remained schematic.

Mercator's 1569 projection solved a specific problem for navigators: on his grid, rhumb lines (lines of constant compass bearing) appear as straight lines, so a sailor could lay a straightedge on two points and read the compass course. The cost was severe geographic distortion at high latitudes. For the problem it was designed for, this was an acceptable trade.

It is worth noting that modern digital mapping largely abandons projection choices to the user. A web map can render itself in Mercator, equal-area, or any other projection on the fly. This erodes the social fact that projections used to impose on entire generations of readers.

Filler about fermentation. The transformation of grapes into wine, milk into yogurt, and cabbage into kimchi is among the oldest biotechnology humans have practiced. In each case microorganisms colonize a substrate, outcompete spoilage organisms by acidifying or alcohol-producing the environment, and produce secondary compounds that give the product its characteristic flavor and preservation properties.

Lactic acid bacteria, particularly species of Lactobacillus and Leuconostoc, dominate most vegetable and dairy ferments. They thrive in slightly anaerobic conditions and tolerate the low pH they themselves produce, which excludes most pathogens. This is why a successful sauerkraut does not require refrigeration for the duration of its primary fermentation.

The study of fermentation moved from art to science largely through the work of Louis Pasteur in the 19th century, who demonstrated that specific microorganisms caused specific fermentations. Before Pasteur, fermentation was considered a spontaneous chemical process. After, it was understood as a biological one, with profound consequences for medicine, industrial chemistry, and food safety.

Modern fermentation-derived products extend well beyond food. Insulin, rennet used in cheesemaking, and many pharmaceutical intermediates are produced by engineered microbes. The economics of microbial production often outcompete chemical synthesis for complex molecules whose stereochemistry would be expensive to control otherwise.
